title: Scientists Remake a Cup That Changes Colour
summary: About 1,600 years ago, Roman artists made a glass cup that changes colour. Now scientists have finally learned how to make it again. The Lycurgus Cup sits in the British Museum in London. It is one of only 40 glass cage cups that still exist. In normal light, the cup looks jade green. But if you shine a light through it, it glows ruby red. The answer is tiny bits of gold and silver mixed into the glass. These bits are thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. They are called nanoparticles. Lisa Hollands, a scientist at the University of Sheffield, worked to crack the recipe. At last she found a mix that works. Her glass looks green in normal light and glows red when light shines through. Glass artist Elliot Walker used the new glass to make a sculpture for the university's Festival of the Mind on November 6. The science may also help make new materials that control light, and special glass for storing dangerous waste safely.
why_it_matters: Old things can teach us new science, and you can see the magic cup change colour in a museum.
